newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Economists caution against Serbian bank monopolies.
newsitem.headline: Economists caution against Serbian bank monopolies.

text.p: Serbia is moving towards creating a banking monopoly after the country's largest bank group, Beogradska Banka, last week unified the international payment and credit operations of its member firms, analysts said on Tuesday.

They cautioned that fostering a monopoly, under the pretext of a major overhaul in the ailing banking sector, could prove damaging for Serbia which has said it aims to create a liberal and open market economy.

"Monopolising the banking sector has no economic excuse. We insist on a market economy but we keep on creating monopolies," Slobodan Milosavljevic, economist with the IZIT Market Research Institute, told Reuters.

Beogradska Banka system, grouping 20 out of 100 Yugoslav banks and servicing almost two-thirds of the Serbian economy, last week set up a new Beogradska Banka Group (BB-Group) with centralised international payment and credit operations.
The bank said it needed to concentrate funds to cut costs and increase the group's capital base to provide more finances for the country's moribund economy.
But analysts fear that creating a giant with centralised control over credit activities may eventually choke private enterprise due to highly-selective access to funds.
"All the money will go to one central account and whoever needs a credit will have to knock on one door. And one needs to be politically correct to qualify for funds," one analyst said.

Apart from centralising dinar funds, Beogradska plans to restructure its European activities and concentrate its capital held in several joint stock banks in Europe into the London-based Anglo-Yugoslav Bank Ltd.

Beogradska is a majority shareholder in five joint stock banks in Europe, including Anglo-Yugoslav Bank Ltd., Banque Franco-Yougoslave in Paris, Adria Bank in Vienna, LHB Internationale Handelsbank AG in Frankfurt and Societe Generale-Yugoslav Bank in Belgrade.

"The idea to pool funds into Anglo-Yugoslav will help the bank attract fresh foreign funds to (the) Yugoslav economy and engage in restructuring the country's external debt," new head of Anglo-Yugoslav Bank Ljubisa Igic said.
After concentrating the capital, Anglo-Yugoslav will spread its network around the European Union, creating more direct access to European and world capital markets, Igic said.

Although some bankers supported the idea to transfer hard currency held by state banks and companies abroad into one place, analysts said the move would be incomplete if capital which fled the country during years of sanctions is not included.

"Capital held on private accounts by those individuals who were politically active over past years must also be included. The money should be transferred to Yugoslav banks' accounts and used for the country's economic revival," said another economist.
Some economists feared that a new banking giant may become too powerful and begin challenging monetary authorities.
"It is unclear what the central bank will do. By creating a powerful Serbian-controlled bank, Yugoslavia's central bank will get a fierce competition," an economist said.

Bank centralisation in Serbia remains incomplete, however, with the largest commercial bank, Beobanka, refusing to accept the BB-Group's plans to deprive it of independent international credit and payment operations.

Although Beobanka said it was conducting its own bank overhaul programme with the help of international consultants, analysts said the move signalled a deep rift over money matters between the ruling Socialists and their junior coalition partner Yugoslav Left which is reported to have influence over Beobanka. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
